This applies whether or not Flathub is targeted, because the disclosure affects every commit and contributor.
options.rationale: It is the only posture that keeps the discretionary Flathub channel reachable without pretending, it costs a statement and a review boundary rather than a change of method, and it is the honest answer for a project that is in fact being built this way.

options.label: No AI-generated material
options.description: Prohibit AI-generated code, docs and packaging outright. Simplest possible answer to every policy question, and it discards the development method this project is being built with.

options.label: Use AI, no disclosure
options.description: Develop as convenient and publish no statement. Least overhead, and it forecloses Flathub (whose review is discretionary and can reject on the extent of generated material) while leaving contributors guessing.

questions.question: Which distribution channels ship with the first release?
questions.grounding: engineering-baseline/references/packaging-and-distribution.md (Flathub rejects console software and needs a tagged release history; Homebrew needs notarization, a repo at least 30 days old, and any one of 90 forks / 90 watchers / 225 stars for a self-submission — 30 / 30 / 75 if someone else submits — plus a download cooldown for some ecosystems that rules out promising same-day brew install); tech-stack-evaluation SKILL.md open decisions 13, 15 and 23

options.label: Releases, AUR, deb/rpm (Recommended)
options.description: GitHub Releases with checksums, an AUR source and -bin pair, and a hosted apt/dnf repo. Covers Linux desktop and headless immediately, since Flathub will not accept console software anyway. Fix the Linux glibc and WebKitGTK floors here by pinning the CI build container in the first workflow file.
options.rationale: It is the only set available on day one — Flathub needs a tagged release history and Homebrew needs notarization plus a repo older than 30 days and one of its notability numbers — and shipping this breadth first is exactly what makes Flathub optional rather than critical.

options.label: Flathub once tags exist
options.description: Submit the GUI to Flathub after a sustained commit history and tagged releases exist, with a human-authored submission PR per q12.1. Widest reach on Linux and where both High Tide and sone are listed; review is discretionary, and the exclusive-output confinement question in q5.3 has to be answered before the UI can tell the truth about it.

options.label: Windows MSI and winget
options.description: Makes Windows first-class from the first release. Decide the WebView2 install mode here — downloadBootstrapper (0 MB, needs network at install) through fixedVersion (~180 MB, freezes the webview build); default to the evergreen bootstrapper and set the floor at Windows 10 April 2018 or later, which is where WebView2 is preinstalled. Without signing, SmartScreen warns on every install.

options.label: macOS DMG, Homebrew later
options.description: A notarized DMG now, with a Homebrew cask once the age and notability thresholds are met. Decide universal (Intel + Apple Silicon) versus Apple-Silicon-only here: a universal build roughly doubles build time and artifact size and requires every bundled native library, including the whole GStreamer or libmpv tree from q5.2, to itself be universal. Without notarization, macOS downloads are effectively unusable and no cask is possible.

questions.question: Who pays for code signing, and from when?
questions.condition: the answer follows q1.2 — a Linux-first v1 defers most of this cost
questions.grounding: engineering-baseline/references/packaging-and-distribution.md §5-§6 (Apple Developer Program $99/yr covering Developer ID and notarization; Azure Trusted Signing reported at $9.99/mo Basic; EV certificate roughly $280-500/yr on a hardware token; Trusted Signing certificates are non-exportable; eligibility is narrower for individuals — organisations in a listed set of countries, individual developers US or Canada only, no free/trial Azure subscriptions, individual onboarding reportedly paused and new organisation customers needing three years of verifiable history). The pricing and eligibility text comes from a search index over Microsoft's pages, not a direct fetch — re-verify before budgeting.

options.label: Both platforms, budgeted (Recommended)
options.description: Apple Developer Program plus a Windows signing certificate, in place before the first binary release on those platforms. Roughly $220/year if Azure Trusted Signing is available to you, or roughly $380-600/year if you must buy an EV certificate — check the eligibility gate first (US or Canada for an individual, a paid Azure subscription, three years of history for a new organisation, individual onboarding possibly paused). Trusted Signing certificates cannot be exported, so losing eligibility means losing the ability to sign.
options.rationale: Unsigned builds are not merely untidy: without notarization there is no Homebrew cask and macOS downloads are effectively unusable, and without Windows signing SmartScreen warns on every install — so the alternative is shipping two of the three named platforms in a state most users cannot get past.

options.label: macOS notarization only
options.description: Pay for Apple at $99/year, accept SmartScreen warnings on Windows. Fixes the platform where unsigned is closest to unusable, and sidesteps the Trusted Signing eligibility question entirely.

options.label: Neither for v1
options.description: Ship Linux properly and treat Windows and macOS as best-effort unsigned builds. No recurring cost, and a bad first impression on two of the three named platforms — consistent only with a Linux-first answer to q1.2.

questions.question: How do installed copies of streamboat get updated?
questions.grounding: tidal-oss-landscape SKILL.md open decision 9 and tech-stack-evaluation SKILL.md open decision 14 (the Tauri updater covers only AppImage, .app.tar.gz and MSI+NSIS; an in-app updater is never acceptable on Flatpak, Snap, AUR or Nix, where the package manager owns the binary); engineering-baseline SKILL.md open decision 5 (update check on by default for source/manual installs, off for managed packages)

options.label: Check and notify only (Recommended)
options.description: Managed packages update themselves; self-contained bundles check a version endpoint and tell the user, linking to the release. The check is on by default for source and manual installs and compiled out or defaulted off for managed packages, and it is a plain HTTPS request with no identifying payload.
options.rationale: It is the only mechanism that is correct on every channel streamboat actually ships to: a self-updating binary is wrong on Flatpak, Snap, AUR, Nix and any distro package, and the Tauri updater covers only three of the bundle formats anyway. Notifying costs one endpoint and no signing key infrastructure.

options.label: Signed updater for bundles
options.description: A signed in-app updater for AppImage, the macOS .app and MSI/NSIS installs, disabled everywhere a package manager owns the binary. Best experience for users who downloaded a bundle directly, at the cost of an update signing key, an appcast feed and a second release-artifact pipeline.

options.label: No update mechanism
options.description: No check and no updater; users learn about releases from the repository or their package manager. Zero code and zero outbound requests, and manual installs quietly go stale — which matters more than usual for a client whose API can change under it.

rounds.title: First milestone, testing and repository shape
rounds.rationale: The crate layout, the definition of 'done' for the first milestone and the provenance of every test fixture must exist before Cargo.toml does. Fixture provenance in particular is a one-way door once real captures are in public git history.

questions.question: What is the first milestone that counts as done?
questions.condition: given the release shape chosen in q1.1 — this is sequencing inside that release, not a change to its scope
questions.grounding: headless-and-tidal-connect SKILL.md staged path steps 1-6; tech-stack-evaluation/references/architecture-shapes.md §4 (the transport is picked at bootstrap from day one)

options.label: Playable spike, then UI (Recommended)
options.description: Log in, resolve a manifest and play one track to the end from the CLI, through the same Command/Event types the GUI will use, with the audio engine already behind its trait and the gapless-plus-exclusive combination from q5.4 prototyped. No browse UI yet.
options.rationale: The manifest-to-DAC path carries every unknown that could invalidate the architecture — encrypted-manifest refusal, DASH parsing, device negotiation, the engine-choice conflict, and the untried gapless-with-exclusive-writer claim — so proving it end to end first is what makes the remaining decisions cheap to act on.

options.label: Auth and browse UI first
options.description: Login plus search and library screens with playback stubbed. Shows visible progress early, validates the UI direction from round 4, and defers every audio unknown to a point where they are more expensive to be wrong about.

options.label: Daemon and CLI first
options.description: A working streamboatd with the control API, MPRIS and device-code login before any GUI. Fastest path to a usable Pi player, with the desktop shell arriving late enough that GUI-shaped requirements can force protocol changes.

questions.question: What is the binary shape that gets installed and packaged?
questions.grounding: tech-stack-evaluation SKILL.md open decision 24 (unreconciled naming between architecture-shapes.md and headless-connect.md — pick one before Cargo.toml exists); headless-and-tidal-connect/references/daemon-architecture.md §1 (librespot's crate boundaries as the model for where core ends)

options.label: streamboat + streamboatd (Recommended)
options.description: Two artifacts: streamboat, the desktop shell with CLI subcommands, and streamboatd, a webview-free daemon. A CI job builds streamboatd in a container with no GTK or WebKit to prove it. The internal crate split behind them (whether the engine is its own crate) follows from q2.2 and is a rename, not a redesign.
options.rationale: It resolves the open naming conflict, and the two-artifact split is the half a CI job can actually enforce — building the daemon in a GUI-free container is what stops the headless path silently regressing into a desktop dependency.

options.label: One binary, daemon subcommand
options.description: Ship a single streamboat binary where 'streamboat daemon' is a mode, as tidalt does. Simplest to install, document and package, and the webview then links into every install including headless ones — which is exactly what the CI guard above exists to prevent.

questions.question: How much testing and CI at the start?
questions.grounding: engineering-baseline/references/testing-strategy.md (parser/transport split, fixture capture, opt-in live canaries; High Tide and tidal-hifi ship zero automated tests of TIDAL behaviour and python-tidal does not run its suite in CI); tech-stack-evaluation testing notes (tauri-driver has no macOS support — Apple ships no WKWebView WebDriver)

options.label: Unit and fixture tests (Recommended)
options.description: Parser/transport split with recorded API fixtures and wiremock, component tests in the frontend, clippy/fmt/lint gates, and a CI job building the daemon in a GTK/WebKit-free container. Fork-safe: no job requires a secret or a live TIDAL account. No end-to-end UI automation yet.
options.rationale: An unofficial-API client cannot run live credentials in CI, so fixtures against a parser/transport split are where the real defect-catching happens — and the headless container build is the single cheapest test that protects the architecture the whole project rests on. The two most-cited reference clients ship no TIDAL behaviour tests at all, so this is cheap ground to be materially better on.

options.label: Add e2e via tauri-driver
options.description: Also drive the built app on Linux and Windows CI. Catches wiring regressions the unit tests cannot; Apple ships no WKWebView WebDriver, so macOS needs a different workaround or goes uncovered.

options.label: Rust unit tests only
options.description: Minimum viable gate while the shape is still moving. Fastest early, and it lets manifest-parsing and quality-cascade regressions reach releases unnoticed.

questions.question: Where do the API test fixtures come from?
questions.grounding: engineering-baseline SKILL.md open decision 15 and references/testing-strategy.md §2 ('synthetic (structure-preserving, content-invented) vs. real captured TIDAL API responses committed to a public test-fixtures directory — a legal/ToS posture decision, not only a redaction mechanic')

options.label: Synthetic fixtures (Recommended)
options.description: Structure-preserving, content-invented fixtures written by hand from the documented schemas — real field names and shapes, invented titles, artists and IDs. Nothing of TIDAL's catalogue is republished, at the cost of fixtures that can drift from the real wire format unless a live canary test is run against a real account periodically.
options.rationale: It is the same family of decision as the caching line in q6.3 and the play-reporting line in q8.2, and it is a one-way door: once real captured catalogue responses are in public git history they cannot be removed from clones. Synthetic fixtures keep the repository free of a third party's content while still testing every parser branch.

options.label: Real captures, redacted, public
options.description: Capture real responses with a scrub script, redact tokens and user identifiers, and commit them. Highest fidelity to the actual wire format and the fastest way to reproduce a parsing bug, and it republishes TIDAL's catalogue metadata in a public repository.

options.label: Real captures, kept private
options.description: Keep a capture script in the repository and the captures themselves gitignored, so each developer generates their own from their own account. Full fidelity with nothing republished, and CI cannot run those tests — which puts the parser tests back in the same place they started.

already_decided: Target platforms: desktop Linux, Windows and macOS AND a headless/server/CLI mode, both now; mobile is a future target the architecture must not preclude.

streamboat talks to the unofficial api.tidal.com v1/v2 API used by python-tidal/High Tide/sone, requiring the user's own paid TIDAL subscription — the official Developer API's Player module is closed-source, web/iOS/Android only, and cannot run headless, so it cannot be the playback spine.
The official openapi.tidal.com/v2 API may be used opportunistically for metadata, playlists, lyrics and ISRC/UPC lookup with the same Bearer token — no second login is required.

streamboat is a player for subscribers, never a downloader or ripper: no DRM circumvention, no OLD_AES or Widevine handling, no credential pooling, no export path, no playback without a logged-in subscriber.

Encrypted manifests (encryptionType != NONE, a non-empty encryptionKey, or securityType/securityToken) are refused loudly with an explanation pointing at the client-ID setting; hi-res tiers are filtered out of the cascade pre-emptively so users rarely hit the wall.
TIDAL Connect is permanently out of scope in both directions — no target, no controller. Only the public positioning around it is still open (q10.3).
Never redistribute a vendor's proprietary binary or device certificate.

One TIDAL account = one concurrent stream, enforced by TIDAL's Pushkin channel: multiroom must be one daemon holding the single stream and fanning PCM out to endpoints, never one daemon per room. Whether and how streamboat speaks that protocol is q10.1.
streamboat-core carries no UI, no windowing and no desktop-OS dependency; the daemon is built as a separate Cargo artifact that must not link a webview, enforced by CI.
The GUI reaches the engine only through the same Command/Event types the control API exposes — there is no private path into the engine.
Every listener binds loopback by default; LAN exposure is a deliberate, logged, token-protected opt-in, paired with Host-header allowlisting.
No telemetry to the project's developers and no hosted crash reporting: local crash dumps plus a 'generate debug bundle' command, with redaction by construction rather than by review.

The forge is GitHub (github.com/Waayway/streamboat). Flathub io.github.* app-ID verification, private vulnerability reporting and CI secret scoping all follow from it; only the owner/app-ID within GitHub is still open (q2.4).
360 Reality Audio is dead (removed by TIDAL 2024-07-24) and must not be implemented; Dolby Atmos is not decoded locally — at most a passthrough flag kept in the manifest-request layer for later.
MQA/HI_RES-era content is gone from the service; the tier is not a product target.
adaptive=false on every manifest request — mid-track representation switching means a format change, a device reopen and an audible gap.
Play reporting, when enabled, is suppressed for PREVIEW assets; assetPresentation != FULL is a distinct playback state with its own UI.

Never claim the tidal:// URI scheme — Strawberry's OAuth redirect, sone/High Tide deep links and TIDAL's own desktop app all register it. Use streamboat:// for both the OAuth redirect and content deep links.
Never link fdk-aac: it is GPL-incompatible and non-distributable alongside GPL parts. AAC decoding, if built, goes through LGPL FFmpeg's avdec_aac or faad.
Strings are externalised from the first commit and a complete English localisation ships; the user's real locale is passed to TIDAL's locale parameter rather than hardcoding en_US.
MPRIS registration lives in the engine, not the GUI, so it works in daemon mode.

Bit-perfect mode bypasses both the volume slider and ReplayGain, and this is stated in the UI rather than implied. 'Bit-perfect' is scoped per track by source type and is never claimed for a lossy AAC source.
